Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

pull oneself together verb

also collect oneself, get a grip, compose oneself

classical

Cic. Tusc. 4.78: quid est autem sē ipsum colligere, nisi dissipātās animī partēs rūrsum in suum locum cōgere? (Lewis & Short s.v. colligō)
Caes. BC 3.65: sē ex timōre (colligere; Lewis & Short)
Traupman 106: pull oneself together, sē colligere

sē colligere

reflexive: mē colligō, tē collige

pull oneself together, recover one’s composure

“To gather oneself together”: Cicero explains it as bringing the scattered parts of the mind back into place. Lewis & Short calls it very frequent and classical; so also animum colligere.

Other words

  • animam recipere — catch one’s breath, recover oneself

    also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 323–325: Quid festīnās, mī Geta? Animam recipe.; Liv. 2.50.10: ā pavōre animum (recipere; Lewis & Short s.v. recipiō)

    Animam recipere is to get one’s breath back; animum recipere, in Livy, to recover from a fright.

See also calm down.

SourcesLewis & Short: colligo · Lewis & Short: recipio
